events.summary: Country: Afghanistan Sources: Asia Pacific Gender in Humanitarian Action Working Group, UN Women Please refer to the attached Infographic. This snapshot presents findings from the sixteenth round of the GCG and HAWG survey on the impact of the bans and other gender-related restrictions on Afghan women working for NGOs, INGOs and the UN. Responses were collected from 7 to 26 October 2026 from 90 organizations: 72 NNGOs and CSOs (62 of them WLOs), 10 INGOs and 8 UN agencies. This round has more respondents working on GBV (60%, from 44% in June) and on human rights and gender equality (69%, from 59%). Restrictions on women's participation in humanitarian and BHN operations remain widespread, despite a decline in reports of new formal instructions. While 36% of organizations reported no new instructions or impediments, practical barriers persist: half report that women staff cannot report to the office in some provinces, and 32% report women staff stopped by the PVPV on the way to work, the highest level across all rounds. Only 42% remain fully operating with women and men, and fewer hold agreements with the DfA for women to work at project locations and offices. With 66% accepting DfA conditions to keep operating, the findings suggest a shift from new formal restrictions towards more persistent enforcement.

Uganda National Baseline Survey on School Feeding (December 2025)
events.summary: Country: Uganda Source: Government of Uganda Please refer to the attached file. Uganda’s National Baseline Survey on School Feeding provides a comprehensive national picture of the coverage, quality and delivery of school meals in primary schools. Led by the Ministry of Education and Sports , the survey establishes an important evidence base to inform policy, programming, investment and future monitoring of school feeding across the country. The findings show that 46 percent of primary school learners receive school meals , with significant disparities across regions and school types. Coverage is highest in Karamoja, Kampala and Buganda North , and lowest in Tooro, Ankole and West Nile , while rural, public and day schools generally have lower coverage. Critically, around 30 percent of learners do not eat any meal while at school , highlighting the continued challenge of hunger during the school day. The report also identifies gaps in dietary diversity, financing, procurement, infrastructure and management, and recommends expanding coverage in underserved areas, improving the nutritional quality of meals, strengthening local procurement and financing, and integrating school feeding more systematically into national education planning and monitoring.

Abstract/Description Flood Early Warning Bulletins translate forecasts into clear, timely, actionable information for preparedness, anticipatory action, and emergency response. By presenting expected conditions, potential impacts, and recommended actions in a standard format, they help government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and at-risk communities coordinate decisions before floods occur. Yet fragmented datasets, disconnected modelling workflows, and manual processes often delay bulletins and shorten the time available to protect lives, livelihoods, and infrastructure. To address this gap, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), national government institutions, and development partners developed the Dolo Ado Digital Twin-based Flood Early Warning System. It creates a digital replica of the floodplain, enables two-way data exchange with communities, and integrates global databases, field surveys, and district data. Recognizing this reality, designing solutions to protect them, and committing to ways of working that do not perpetuate threats to women's lives and well-being is one of our priorities. In this article, we share recommendations for delivering a safe, dignified humanitarian response that avoids revictimization. When an emergency or disaster strikes, institutional and community support networks weaken, livelihoods are disrupted, and pre-existing inequalities and vulnerabilities deepen. As a result, in crisis-affected settings, up to 70% of women experience violence, nearly double the rate recorded outside crisis zones. The challenge is even more urgent given global gaps in violence prevention and care. events.title: Cameroon Cholera Outbreak: Situation Report #8 (November 25, 2026)
events.summary: Country: Cameroon Source: International Medical Corps Please refer to the attached file. FAST FACTS 462 suspected cholera cases and four deaths (0.87% CFR) were recorded in Minawao Refugee Camp between July 24 and October 17, with zero new cases for 29 consecutive days as of November 15. Minawao hosts more than 81,000 refugees—more than triple its intended capacity (325%)—resulting in an attack rate of 570 cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Across Cameroon’s Far North Region, 3,038 cases (15% in Minawao) and 86 deaths (2.83% case-fatality rate) were recorded across 18 health districts as of November 9, with the last regional case reported on October 28. Though active cholera transmission inside Minawao has stopped, the wider regional outbreak has not yet been declared over. Overcrowding, cross-border mobility and unresolved water and sanitation gaps sustain the risk of reintroduction into the camp. OUR RESPONSE Operating in Minawao Refugee Camp since 2013, International Medical Corps launched an emergency cholera response within 24 hours of the initial alert on July 24, supporting the Mokolo Health District with pre-positioned contingency stocks. We expanded the camp’s existing 15-bed treatment unit to 100 beds using temporary overflow tents and 37 clinical and support staff. We trained, equipped and supervised 90 refugee community health workers (CHWs) across all camp blocks, who conducted 140,000+ household visits, traced 3,400+ contacts, and disinfected 8,000+ households and community spaces. Deployed all 90 CHWs as volunteer vaccinators—helping to reach 75,444 people (92.6% coverage)—and documented operational lessons to strengthen readiness for future outbreaks.

events.title: Conflict Response in Baidoa, Somalia: Situation Report #2 (November 25, 2026)
events.summary: Country: Somalia Source: International Medical Corps Please refer to the attached file. FAST FACTS The conflict in Baidoa, Somalia, has resulted in significant damage to civilian infrastructure and public buildings while displacing residents and increasing humanitarian needs across the district. The deteriorating security situation has disrupted access to essential services, including healthcare, and increased the number of displaced people seeking assistance. Control of several territories has changed, further raising tensions in Baidoa. OUR FOOTPRINT International Medical Corps has operated in Somalia since 1990, providing a wide range of humanitarian and health services, including primary and secondary healthcare, health workforce training, health education, emergency response, mental health and psychosocial support, nutrition, protection, community empowerment, and water, sanitation and hygiene services. OUR RESPONSE International Medical Corps has deployed two primary health units to provide integrated health and nutrition services to internally displaced persons and vulnerable host communities in Baidoa. We established a standby emergency response team to support Bay Regional Hospital during mass-casualty incidents and conflict-related emergencies. Ongoing projects have delivered lifesaving nutrition support to drought-affected communities in rural villages across Baidoa district, helping residents who displaced by the conflict in Baidoa benefit from these services.

events.title: World: Protecting Children from Air Pollution: Applying the social and behaviour change message guidance in the REACH Framework
events.summary: Country: World Source: UN Children's Fund Please refer to the attached file. Highlights Air pollution is the single biggest environmental threat to child health. Around 930 million children, 4 in 10 worldwide, breathe outdoor air with a level of fine particles seven times that considered safe by the World Health Organization. Every day, almost 2,000 children under 5 years of age die from air-pollution-related causes, accounting for more than one in four of all deaths in this age group. Three quarters of these deaths are linked to air pollution inside the home. Yet it's one of the hardest risks to communicate, because the harm is invisible, cumulative, and easily normalized. This new guide offers a framework for messages that move families and decision makers from awareness to sustained protective action, organized around the REACH (recognize, engage, act, context, habit) framework and designed to be localized to each setting.

events.title: Central African Republic: Overview of incidents affecting humanitarian workers (october 2026)
events.summary: Country: Central African Republic Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached file. Since January 2026, 96 incidents have affected humanitarian workers in the Central African Republic. In October, 12 incidents were reported, compared to 14 in September, a decrease of 14 percent. Out of 12 incidents recorded in October, six were criminal in nature, including three cases of theft, two robberies and one assault. For the first time in 2026, a humanitarian worker was killed in an incident involving armed individuals. Five other incidents involved restrictions including movement restrictions, requests for documentation, arrest, taxation, and a protest targeting an NGO. The Birao sub-prefecture was the most affected with four incidents, followed by Bangui with three incidents. The sub-prefectures of Bocaranga, Bossangoa, Alindao and Obo each recorded one incident. International NGOs were the most affected, with eight incidents recorded, followed by UN agencies and national NGOs with two incidents each. Since January 2026, the Vakaga prefecture remains the most affected, with 24 incidents recorded, followed by Bangui with 21 incidents and Haut-Mbomou with 17 incidents.

An estimated 620 children are currently out of school. SOS Children’s Villages Somalia conducted a field visit and community dialogue in four IDP locations in Lafoole (Waafi, Docol, Durdur and Takulo) to verify the presence of newly displaced families, understand education and protection needs, and identify potential FLER sites. The assessment identified 402 newly displaced households. Education is the most urgent gap: existing public schools are located approximately 1 km to more than 3 km from the settlements, and children who remain out of school face heightened risks of abuse, neglect, exploitation, child labour, family separation, early marriage and psychosocial distress. Immediate FLER activation is therefore strongly justified. FLER will provide safe, structured learning, psychosocial support, play and life-skills activities, foundational learning and protection identification and referral, while creating a pathway into neighbouring schools. Docol and Durdur IDP Community Centres are the priority FLER locations, covering multiple surrounding IDP subcamps.

events.title: World: Preparedness for the next crisis means planning for the one after it
events.summary: Country: World Source: ODI - Humanitarian Practice Network Giuseppe Saba As the escalation of hostilities in Lebanon in March 2026 intensified humanitarian needs and displacement, the ability to respond quickly depended in part on decisions made before the emergency. By 1 May 2026, UNHCR reported that, together with shelter sector partners, it had delivered relief items to more than 200,000 displaced people, largely using pre-positioned supplies. Additional support included 40 trucks carrying more than 317 metric tonnes of critical aid from Dubai . Preparedness enabled the response. Stocks, logistics infrastructure and multiple transport options were available before the operating environment deteriorated. This flexibility is increasingly essential in humanitarian logistics. Conflict can escalate while teams are responding to floods elsewhere; a disease outbreak can increase demand as border restrictions constrain supply; and disruption to a single transport route can affect operations far beyond the crisis that caused it. Overlapping emergencies place simultaneous pressure on the same people, supplies, funding and logistics networks. Preparedness must therefore preserve the capacity to adapt under pressure. That requires strategically positioned supplies, alternative routes and suppliers, visibility of available stocks, established cross-sector relationships, and mechanisms that link early warning to early action. These options need to be in place before a response is under strain. Prepare for crises that overlap Other operational lessons from the past six years began with Covid-19. Nairobi, 24 November 2026 – International non-governmental organisations working in Sudan remain alarmed by the escalating use of drones and its toll on civilians. According to the UN Human Rights Office, at least 2,230 civilians were killed between January and October 2026, more than 1,630 of them in drone strikes, and the toll is likely higher. Drone strikes also continue to damage the infrastructure civilians need to survive and to disrupt life-saving assistance. Recent incidents in Nyala and Khartoum have again put civilians, including humanitarian personnel, in harm’s way. On 19 November, multiple strikes reportedly hit the Al Mazad district of Nyala, South Darfur, a civilian area close to humanitarian premises. On 22 November, drone strikes in Khartoum damaged a UN premises in a residential neighbourhood while personnel were inside. These incidents are not isolated. This is the Forum’s seventh alert on drone strikes this year. Attacks directed at civilians, including humanitarian personnel, and indiscriminate attacks are prohibited under International Humanitarian Law (IHL). While the targets and circumstances of these attacks have not been independently verified, all parties must distinguish between civilian objects and military objectives. They must take all feasible precautions to protect civilians from the effects of attacks and, to the extent feasible, avoid locating military objectives within or near densely populated areas, including humanitarian premises. For many women and girls living with and at-risk of HIV, violence does not stop at home. It follows them into schools, online, clinics, maternity wards and even into courtrooms. Violations of bodily autonomy and reproductive rights not only cause lasting harm but also undermines trust in health systems, creating barriers to accessing HIV prevention, treatment and care and support. Women and girls living with HIV have been documenting these violations for decades and demanding accountability. "Justice must reach the places where violence happens, including our health systems," said Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS. "No woman should be sterilized without her informed consent, denied the right to make decisions about her own body or be prosecuted for feeding her child. Women living with HIV deserve dignity, care and protection—not coercion, punishment or fear. Governments must end impunity and ensure justice for survivors." Only 56.3% of women aged 15–49 years who are married or in a union have full decision-making power over sex, contraception and reproductive healthcare, falling to 36.8% in sub-Saharan Africa.
